p: But so you'd have to take some paper and some online and combine them, right, for the tracking.

Yeah, we, we can convey to the Department of Ed, should they want, what, what and whom, how much registrations we've had this year alone or next year. That's, that's the ultimate goal of it, which, which we've—
It's just about— I don't think it's an impossible task. What it is, is it's about breaking an old habit.
Yeah.

People are used to doing it this way and used to handing out the forms. And, you know, we need to get to the point where the, the younger folks, especially whether it's school students or, you know, millennials as they say, have to know that they can pick up their cell phone and do it right from their cell phone.

I'm aware of that, but I'm just— well, it's not going to be cell phone in the high schools, Mike, in case you didn't know, but it could be, uh, laptop. So I think we should work— we'll work with DOE to try to get them to do it but as long— you can count. Somebody may still do it on paper. We put the two together, you gotta—
Right.
It's not hard.
Correct.

One plus the other is what the total is. All right, so that's something to work on for us. Um, homeless people who are housing

instability situations. Obviously it's hard for them to receive voter information. Voter registration forms ask for an address. I think you can vote without having a permanent address, but please answer that. What steps have you taken to deal and get people who are homeless to understand that they can vote? And, um, what guidance is provided to poll workers when somebody comes in, when they do list a shelter or is it park bench? I've seen that. Um, do you coordinate with the outreach, uh, workers at different shelters? Have you conducted outreach to city shelters or to supportive housing facilities? And again, do you have data? That's another place where you collect data on this issue.

Yeah, so the education part of that is the, uh, we work with, uh, the Campaign Finance Board because that falls into, uh, their responsibility, and we provide them, uh, with updated information to make sure that, you know, uh, that Madam Chair may remember a few years back when there was some misinformation that was promulgated with respect to, uh, who was eligible to vote if they were, uh, a convicted felon. And we worked with the Campaign Finance Board to make sure that they had uh,

the correct and updated information to avoid that from happening again in the future. Um, and in, in similar regard, when there are, um, outreach requirements that the, the, the Campaign Finance Board has, we, uh, have worked, uh, very closely with them to make sure that they have the accurate information. In terms of, uh, special, uh, instructions to the poll poll workers. The system, the registration system, is designed to accommodate, uh, people who don't have a permanent address, and it's in the system. So as long as— if the person shows up to vote, uh, there's nothing that really needs to be done on the part of the poll worker. They show up to vote, they give them their— if their name, it comes up on, on the iPad, uh, they sign their signature uh, and move on.
Right and, but in terms of there's no tracking for those who are in shelters or in, I would just call temporary housing, there's no tracking for that?
There's not.

No and, and again, similar to the incarcerated population, that is also a very transient population within the City of New York. Uh, so I, I honestly can't see how we could implement an effective tracking system, uh, that involves individuals who may be, uh, on the move on a regular basis.

Alright, I thank you very much. I would look forward to dealing with that one school that is quite upset and trying to find another location. We can work with you on that if you want, and then, um, you know, we work with you on your capital needs that are more immediate with your vans, and then just look forward to, um, getting as many people as possible to vote. I think obviously in the last election many more people did vote but what was the new number that you had in terms of voting for last election?
Uh, it was north of 2 million.
North of 2 million, okay, alright.
I don't know the exact number, right, which is, uh, that was in the mail.

I do have one more question. Thank you for reminding me. Council Member Dinowitz has a question. He's - I forgot that he's, uh, had a question. Let me read to you right now. Hold on, hold on. Yeah, I know. I'm just trying to find it. Here it is. Okay. It is. Thank you for reminding me. I think he sent a letter to you in 2024 outlining the concerns about the way party positions appear on primary election ballots, and he didn't get a response. So number 1, party positions such as District leader, state Committee appear on the primary ballot when there's a contested primary. How -historically there were two seats for each position within an assembly district, one designed for a male and one designed for a female, and the ballots reflected that structure. Male and female candidates were listed separately and voters were instructed to vote for one candidate for each seat. More recently, the rules governing these positions were changed so that the two winners must be the top vote-getters of different genders. However, the ballots have not been updated to reflect this change.

At this current time, all candidates appear under a single heading regardless of gender, even though two candidates of the same gender cannot both win the seats. That's for sure. This creates confusion for voters and candidates alike because the ballot does not clearly communicate how the winners are actually determined. So the question is, will the Board of Elections commit to updating its ballot design so that party official candidates are clearly separated by gender and the ballot explicitly states that only one candidate from each gender may be elected for a maximum of 2 positions? Only Council Member Dinowitz could think of this question.

So, uh, that, that may be, uh, the, the, the impression, but I can tell you without naming names that one of the board's commissioners, uh, agrees in some respects, uh, with Councilman Dinowitz. The difficulty here is, and the short answer is to the councilman's question is no. And the reason— no, we will not be changing and the reason is not because we want to be obstreperous or we want to

create difficulty, but what's not being factored into that question is X.
Right.

Right, so if, if the question was we have two variables, male or female, then the question is is more straightforward. When you add in X and turn 2 variables into 3 variables, um, there's really nothing, uh, that the city board can do about it and have been so instructed by the State Board of Elections. Uh, you know, I think one misconception that I always try to beat back is that we simply have a free hand to do whatever we want. The state legislature, uh, tells us to do things, uh, the state board of elections, and in this particular case did tell us how we have to do it, and we follow what they're telling us. And from time to time, this body, uh, has, uh, made enactments that tell us to do things. So we're not just, you know, freehandedly doing whatever we feel like doing. So we follow the state law, we follow the state board of elections guidance and directive in this regard. And, you know, unless and until there are changes in one of those two

areas, uh, we're going to continue to do things the way that we've been doing them.

Well, I mean, Council Member Dinowitz spends much more time. I just get elected and win, so I don't— my question is, so you could end up with two men or two women or an X and a— because then that's not how the process works. You have to have— it could be X and a man or whatever but I guess when you end up voting in this situation— I have not paid attention like he has—
So, to make it -
To end up with situations, to make it viable.
To make it simple, uh, and, and by the way, the party rules—
There's a party bylaw—
And the party rules and bylaws factor into this as well. But in, in— because the councilman is a Democrat, we'll stick with the Democrats. If it were, say, 3 people running for a party position -
Correct.
Two women and a man. We'll leave X out of it for now. Both women can't win.
No, they can't.
So if the, if the man gets a vote-
Right.
And the two women get 2,000 votes and 1,500 votes, it's gonna be the one that got the 2,000 votes and the one vote man that voted for himself.
Okay, so it's in the end it works out.
Yeah, short answer is not us.
Exactly.

No, I got it. You're gonna have to talk to the Council Member. Uh, poll— second question: poll site changes result in voter confusion and can have the effect of disenfranchising New Yorkers. What— while the Board of Elections may send out notifications of polling sites, voters who are voting at a different site may require a separate explicit notice that their poll site has changed. Question: will the Board of Elections commit to sending out an additional notification to those voters poll site has changed?
We do.
Or explicitly, explicitly highlight that there's a change in voting sites?

We do send out when there's an alteration, um, and to be clear, all of our poll site alterations at this stage have to be run through the Attorney General's office under the John Lewis Voter Rights Act as well.

Right and, and if the change occurred prior to the annual information going— annual information notice going out, probably for the last— well, Val Vásquez was still there, so I want to say it was 2014, 2015. We reworked the information notice, and there's a banner on the information notice. If your poll site's changed, it tells you right on the outside of the information notice that your poll site has changed.
Okay, okay. He might be talking about if it's the last minute, I don't know.

Well those, uh, poll site change notices are auto-generated when we make the, when we make the change. So everyone, um, who has a, has their poll site change gets a poll site change notice that's auto-generated by the system.
I - poll sites in the mail? You talk about in the mail?
Right, yes.
So, how many people do not open their mail? I'm just saying, it's amazing they don't.
There is a certain level of personal responsibility with that, but it also goes through the Attorney General's office for, uh, for as well, so.
Okay.

Right and so to, to Mr. Ignizio's point, under the John Lewis Voter Rights Act, the Board of Elections, um, has lost, uh, I, maybe I don't want to say it that way, but we don't have as much autonomy as we used to have in terms of poll site moves. And we have to go through a pretty, uh, rigorous process and make the submission to the Attorney General's office. We've worked very closely with them and we have it down to a pretty good science right now, uh, but we can't move a poll site without the approval of the, uh, Attorney General's office unless of course it's a very last-minute thing

like there's a gas leak in a, in a poll site and we have no other choice.
Okay, um, how do you use social media to tell people about these things, about anything?

Um, we robustly use Twitter or X, whatever you call it these days. Um, we use it very frequently. In fact, we've, we've received a lot of accolades over the past several years for informing people on voter hours. We do it every single day that there's voting is open. Um, in the preamble to an election, we let people know, uh, and we send messages throughout, uh, periodically.
You're not allowed to use TikTok, right? Are you allowed to use—
Uh, in accordance with the city regulations, I think the state has the same regulations they were advising against it. I don't know where we are today, but that was as of, you know several -
No, you’re right? But it's crazy because that's where everybody's paying attention, so.
But we do a lot of push notifications, uh, throughout the various platforms.
Okay, TikTok is where they want to go.
I can't help you.
Is that where they want to go?
People want to go there. All my staff, TikTok, TikTok.
Should I, should I not admit for the purposes of this hearing that I've never been on TikTok?
You should admit that-
That's a factor of age.
That's— yeah. I'm on all the time. I love TikTok. Um, do we have a plan for ICE? God forbid they show up at a polling place.
Do, do we?
Yeah, in other words, people are nervous about ICE and obviously I don't know who they'd be looking for because—
I mean, you know, we have NYPD at every, at every poll site.

Yeah, but most people voting are Americans, but they don't seem to care these

days. So the question is, the public is asking, do we have a plan for ICE showing up at a polling place? Would it be part of your training? So, I mean, to me, the answer is you cannot come in here if you don't have a judicial warrant. Get out but I don’t know whether that training is -

Right, overall poll site security is the responsibility of the New York City Police Department. So we work, uh, very closely with the, with the New York City Police Department and if there was an individual, uh, circumstance where, where it was impeding voting, we have mechanisms in place to deal with, uh, circumstances where people are being deprived of the right to vote.
And as per the New York State Constitution, only citizens can vote, so we don't expect, uh, any issue.
No, I know, but it's a question that people are asking generally now these days. Alright, thank you very much for your testimony, and thank you for your—
Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you to the members of the Committee, and thanks to this Council.
Thank you.
Thank you, Madam Chair.

I think we'll hear from OATH next. Yes, okay, OATH's Fiscal '27 Preliminary Budget totals $80.1 million, which is $851,725 less than Fiscal '26 Adopted Budget. As we know, OATH is the city's central independent administrative law court comprised of the trials, hearings, and more recently, special education hearings division. The Preliminary Plan includes no new needs and very minor adjustments to OATH’s budget. I look forward to learning more today about the role in the collection of fines, staffing practices for ALJs, Administrative Law Judges, which I know many, and hearing officers, and how the agency will respond to the Mayor's Savings Mandate, especially given the agency has just 2% vacancy rate. So now we'll swear you in. Thank you.

Alright, we will now hear testimony from OATH. Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation. Panelists, please raise your right hands.

Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this Committee, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Alright, you may begin when ready.

Thank you so much. Good afternoon, Chair Brewer. From the Committee of Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation, my name is Vilda Vera Mayuga, and as Chief Administrative Law Judge and Commissioner of the New York Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, I thank you for the opportunity to testify today about the tribunal's work over the past year and the budget project— projection for this coming year. OATH is New York City's central and independent administrative law tribunal. As I start leading this tribunal, I am confident in our continuing to deliver our mission to ensure due process, fair and impartial hearings and timely decisions for everyone who comes before OATH. In calendar year 2025 alone, we received over 1 million summonses, held over a quarter of a million hearings, issued over 1,800 appeals decisions, conducted over 500 trials, and closed nearly 18,000

special education cases. Overall, this is an increase from the volume of work we did in calendar year 2024. And these tremendous figures are a testament to the amazing public servants who are part of the OATH team. In each of these hundreds of thousands of cases, the committed staff at OATH take great care to ensure that every party who appears before us is treated impartially and is accorded due process. We accomplish this by having administrative law judges and judicial hearing officers who listen to all sides, review the evidence without favor, favor, apply the law fairly, and avoid external influence. At OATH, we believe that there is one standard of justice for all. The members of the public who have cases at OATH are treated no differently from the city agencies that appear before us. We do not take direction from any city agency on our cases. Our role is to adjudicate cases, not to set policy. OATH's Fiscal Year 2026 Adopted Budget was $80.9 million, and the current modified budget is $81.8 million. Preliminary budget for Fiscal Year '27 will be $80.1 million, including $62.7 in personal services and $17.4 in other than personal services. Our authorized headcount, it's set at 470 in Fiscal

Year '27 Preliminary Budget, which does not include the currently active 172 per session judicial hearing officers in the Hearings Division, all of whom work on a part-time schedule. OATH has 3 separate units that conduct adjudications: the Trials Division, the Hearings Division, and the Special Education Hearings Division. The law will generally specify which cases go to which division, and all of them offer in-person and remote options for the parties to appear and present their cases. At the Trials Division, we adjudicate a wide range of cases filed by city agencies, boards, and commissions, Trials are conducted by administrative law judges appointed to 5-year terms, and the division's caseload includes employee discipline and disability hearings for civil servants, as well as cases involving city-issued license suspensions and revocations, city vendor contract disputes, the conflicts of interest law, the city human rights law, consumer and worker protection laws, LOFT law, short-term rentals, press passes, watershed protection, retention of police vehicles prior to forfeiture proceedings, and campaign finance violations.

During the first half of Fiscal Year '26, the trials division heard 152 cases, and more than 94% of the decisions issued by OATH ALJs were adopted by the agency heads who referred those cases to OATH. The hearings division is comprised of adjudications, clerk's office, and appeals. Adjudications conducts hearings on summonses issued by more than 20 different city enforcement agencies for alleged violations of law or city rules. City enforcement agencies that issued these summonses include Building and Sanitation, DEP, Fire, Parks Department, DCWP, Health, the Department's, uh, Finance Office of the Sheriff, and the Taxi and Limousine Commission. During the first half of Fiscal Year '26, the Hearings Division processed over 500,000 summonses, heard over 250,000 cases, and handled 875 appeals. This reflects an increase of 14% in cases heard from the prior year. Although respondents have the option to appear to a hearing in person, most continue to take advantage of our telephonic hearings, a safe, easy, and convenient option. Our clerk's office assists respondents with scheduling remote hearings by email,

and offering a callback option to eliminate the need to wait on hold for the hearing officer to start their case. The Special Education Hearings Division handles filings related to claims for services for students with special needs. Each complaint is assigned to an impartial hearing officer who must adjudicate the matter in a fair and timely manner. As of March 2nd, there have been close to 13,000 cases filed in Fiscal Year '26, and cases do continue to be filed each day. And of those cases filed, the division has closed approximately 6,700 and I am happy to report that 89% of those cases closed this year have been closed within the statutory compliance deadline. Now, since 2016, OSE Center for Creative Conflict Resolution has served as the city's government central resource for conflict resolution services and restorative practices in support of city government agencies, businesses, and the general public. The center offers a number of workplace conflict services for city agencies, including mediations, conflict coaching, group facilitation, restorative circles,

dispute system design services, education, and training. And a primary goal of the center is to support city government agencies and offices build alternative dispute resolution and restorative programs to strengthen agencies' internal conflict resolution capacity, including in their public-facing work. During the past year, the Center has provided close to 500 consultations, coaching sessions, conflict resolution and restorative practices trainings, workplace and community mediations, and group facilitation. Now, OATH's mission requires it to prioritize the public's access to justice, and to do so, OATH ensures Language Access Services serves respondents through the Help Center— sorry, uh, and conducts outreach. OATH ensures information is accessible by providing it in plain language and translating it into the top 10 languages spoken in New York City. Everyone has access to free translation services for Hope sessions, trials, hearings, community service, and mediation.

OATH also makes its forms and applications available in the top 10 languages, as well as other documents such as outreach flyers, informational fact sheets, and handouts. Additionally, OATH provides hearing decisions in any language requested by a respondent free of charge at both of its high-volume adjudicatory divisions, namely the OATH Hearings Division and the Special Education Hearings Division. In fact, the Comptroller audited OATH's language access services in late 2025 and found that OATH had institutionalized language access and was in compliance with all language access laws and regulations. OATH is proud to report that the Comptroller had no recommendations for improvement in this area. Now, not having a lawyer should not limit one's ability to navigate OATH's processes. Without providing legal advice, OATH's Help Center ensures that unrepresented respondents receive answers to their questions, are aware of their rights, and understand the hearing process, engaging with unrepresented respondents in their language of preference via telephone, text, email, and in-person at OATHS offices.

Procedural Justice Coordinators respond to requests for help sessions within 1 calendar day on average. This means that in 2025, the help center staff assisted nearly 150,000 respondents. This is an increase of more than 50,000 when compared to the prior year, and for eligible cases, the help center staff can also refer unrepresented respondents to independent legal services providers for possible representation at an OATH hearing at no cost to the respondent. And the help center did so in close to 250 cases last year. This type of personalized assistance helps OATH ensure that all New Yorkers have access to justice. In addition, OATH's help center has specialized units to focus on assistance to small businesses, veterans, and older adults. And since 2021, the help center began conducting help sessions in OATHS Trials Division for unrepresented for-hire vehicle drivers facing license suspension or revocation and vehicle owners seeking to recover their vehicles after NYPD seizure pursuant to an arrest. More than a dozen explanatory fact sheets on enforcement agency processes and OATHS hearing process are available at the Help Center and can be

translated into the top 10 languages. Understanding that city government can sometimes be challenging to navigate, OATH has various vehicles for keeping respondents and practitioners updated on new developments. This includes the Tribunal's website, our monthly Bench Notes e-newsletter, and as of last fall, the publication of OATH Trials Division case summaries in the New York Law Journal. Committed to bringing greater access to justice to all New Yorkers, OATH continues to leave our offices and visit our city's diverse neighborhoods, educating residents and small businesses about what we do and how New Yorkers and New York City businesses can resolve their civil violations. In the first half of Fiscal Year '26, OATH conducted over 100 public-facing educational events in collaboration with elected officials, business associations, community groups, and more. And these educational events include one of OATH's most successful initiatives, OATH Resource. This involves OATH staff working with Council Members and the Brooklyn, New York, and Queens Public Libraries to assist library visitors on matters related to their summonses and the hearing process.

We are grateful for the collaboration with our libraries and elected officials and look forward to working more with the Council to continue to find ways to ensure New Yorkers have greater access to justice with OATH. Whatever challenges await the city, OATH's amazing staff have dedicated themselves, um, to meeting the moment and making sure that New Yorkers receive impartial hearings and timely decisions. OATH staff is very much New York's fairest. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify before you today. I look forward to our continued collaboration with the City Council, and I welcome any questions you may have.

Thank you. We have lots of questions, but we have to wait a minute while they reset the technology, so thank you. Well, first I wanna thank John Castelli. That's like number one in my world. I know where you're sitting there, sir, but you are awesome. I just wanna say to start with, um, my question just, um, just in terms of savings, obviously May 20th, that's the date that you have to come up with if there are some ways to, um, curtail or cost or revenue.

So are there programs uh, in your budget that are exempt from the savings requirement? And if so, which ones? And can you, even though it's not March 20th yet, do you have any areas where you're considering in this savings exercise? We're all glad to hear about the 2-for-1 hiring policy ending, but it is concerning to hear that agencies will only be permitted to fill out half— to fill half of their current vacancies. You may not have very many vacancies compared to other agencies. So I think you have maybe 13. I don't know if that's still the current number. So are you going to be eliminating some of your vacancies? And if so, uh, what, which ones?

Thank you, Chair Brewer and yes, as, as you mentioned, because we're still, uh, that's due on the 20th, and yes, we are still having a lot of conversations internally trying to meet with the team and try to understand all of the operations of the tribunal so that we can make the right decision on what to propose to OMB and City Hall based on the ask that they've made of us. For OATH, there's no programs per se, right? It's, it's all of the different divisions that do

adjudications, and of course the areas that support, as well as the Center for Creative Conflict Resolution. I don't expect that we'll be cutting any programs, even, you know, wherever we're finding the savings, but it is true that we are still in that process of making some decisions.
And is 13 the right number of vacancies?
We, we have 10.
You have 10.

Yes. Um, the other question I have is, um, you and I spent quite a bit of time closing and we, uh, illegal, I guess, tobacco shops, also known as cannabis shops. They seem to go together and, um, which was great and then I assume most of those went to OATH. I think it was very hard to collect. Now, Finance does the collection. I know, in other words, you adjudicate, this is what your fine is, and then I guess it goes off to Finance because one of the concerns that I have is, you know, Finance is supposedly responsible for the collection of the fine, but we don't know how much is uncollected. And I don't know if there's anything we can do working

together to improve the collection rate because we're all trying to figure out how to have more money in our coffers. And I did a report with IBO a few years ago, it was $2 billion just for that year, hmm, uncollected. Um, so I'm just wondering, I know it's not, I, every time I ask OATH is, oh no, no, it's not my problem, it's Finance. I talk to Finance, they say we can't really do anything. It's frustrating because, you know, those of us, those New Yorkers who pay all their taxes and pay their fines and pay their fees. Then they see other people are not doing it. So I didn't know if there was any discussion going on, um, that it could be a better collection rate.

We haven't had any discussions, and yes, as you mentioned, OATH as a tribunal, you know, we've been the impartial party that adjudicates, does not get involved in collections. If we can be of help in terms of providing information based on just numbers that come to us and the adjudications that we make, we're happy to work with the Council to provide that information that we

may have, but it is true that we do not engage in collection efforts or—

Yeah, it’s not working with the Council so much as working with Finance. In other words, right now is— I just think it's a little bit on the siloed end. You know, there may be some ideas that the ALJs have for how to, uh, best contact that person. That person's gonna leave, you know, your courthouse, so to speak or your online Zoom and they've been assessed X, but sometimes they just don't pay it. So I, I know that Finance has collection agencies and they make phone calls, but I just think some conversation should be going on because maybe the ALJs will have some idea about how to do a better job. I don't know, but it's a big number that's not collected. And the worst of the cannabis, they just took off. Yeah so anyway, I'd love to hear more about that. There's, you know, we're all excited about making sure that people have justice, but they don't pay their fines a lot. So I want more on that. Um, same issue, Environmental Control Board. Uh, those fines make up the largest cohort of unpaid fines and the uncollected revenue. You know, all of

this could be used to close the budget gap. So I didn't know, again, do you talk to the Environmental Control Board? Is there anything OATH can do to help collect those fines? Again, a different body.

Yeah, I mean, we limit ourselves to issuing those decisions, and certainly we do have a lot of reporting that we can share in terms of decisions that we make, what are the— how we adjudicate them, um, what are the results of those. And the enforcement agencies are of course at liberty to then use that information for the next steps based on the decision that the tribunal has issued.

Okay um, and just in terms of online versus in-person, so I guess pandemic, much more online and I think now even there's no pandemic, but I think much of it is online. So I just didn't know, do you need as much staff? How do you supervise? How does it technology— I have a whole bunch of friends who are ALJs. How does— and they're always sitting in their kitchen, I guess. Um, I don't— I think you should come in, but that's okay, alright. So then again, I would assume less space needed. I would assume, uh, you mean more supervision? I don't know. How are you dealing with

this very new, um, I'd like to know the percentage that are doing their work online and I'd like to know what the technology is at home. Can you get into the IT? Some of them say it's sometimes hard to get an IT person. I'm just saying. Because it's, um, you know, people having problems with their home computer. And then also supervision. How do you know it's going well? When you're in the office, you can check.

Can— er, Chair Brewer, first, you know, thank you for caring so much, because certainly these are the issues that I, I also welcome, having just completed my one month at the agency. The majority - so going back to my testimony, right, we have 3 main areas of adjudication, right? You have the trials division where those ALJs are definitely, I mean, I, I'm seeing them all the time in the office, so I know that they're there. And there is, uh, diversity of number of cases that may be in person and some via WebEx for the trials division. We do then have the special education hearings. A lot of those are also via video.
That's Carter, I call that Carter— the Carter cases.

Correct and then we— the biggest, the highest volume, it is the Hearings Division, and that is the one that perhaps you're referring to. Correct. We have a little bit over 30-something in-person hearing officers, right? There are attorneys that work in— 30 in person, you said?
30 in person?

Yes, yes, from the Hearings Division and 33 to be precise, full-time hearing officers. And then we have the per diem hearing officers that, as the word says, right, they work part-time. They have, uh, most of them have a limit of hours that they can work during the year and that number in terms of the active ones is 170 of them. Now, the amount of hours that each of them works varies. It depends, right? We understand a lot of them have other things that they're doing with their professional life, and they might be doing this on the side, or maybe this is all that they were doing, perhaps they retired in their practice. We support them technologically if they have issues because they have to remote into our system. So there are— sometimes we have space issues. Yes, if we wanna have more people come in person or we wanna

have more in-person hearing officers available, but at the same time, we're using all the space in the most creative ways that we can because we still need those judicial hearing officers that are working remotely to remote into our system. And so we do provide them that support as well.

So, uh, but what's the percentage? I said you— a number you gave me, 170. We don't know how many of those are online, right? I mean, what's the percentage of— what I'm trying to find is online versus in person, just in terms of generally for the hearings. I know about the trial in the Carter. In other words, how many of all of your per diems? I guess the 33 are all in person.
Yes.
But of the per diems, that's for—
They're all remote.
They're all remote.
Yes.
Uh, all remote all the time.
